title: The Golden Gate Bridge opened to walkers first: 200,000 crossed in a day

cover.alt: Black-and-white film still from 1937: a dense crowd walks along the empty roadway of the Golden Gate Bridge, with a tall tower behind them in the haze.

body: The opening celebrations began at 6 a.m. on 27 May 1937 and went on for a week. For that first day the new bridge belonged to people, not cars: about **200,000** walked or roller-skated across. The next day President Franklin D. Roosevelt pushed a button in Washington, D.C., and the bridge opened to vehicles at noon. Its 1,280-metre main span was the longest of any suspension bridge in the world until 1964.

slides.alt: Black-and-white film: a huge crowd of men, women and children in 1930s clothes walks towards the camera along the bridge roadway, with one of the towers rising behind them.
slides.caption: Opening celebrations, May 1937: crowds on foot stream along the bridge’s roadway beneath one of its towers.

slides.label: main span, the longest of any suspension bridge until 1964
slides.text: Its towers rise 227 metres (746 feet) above the water, and they stayed the tallest on any suspension bridge until 1993.

slides.prompt: For the bridge’s 50th birthday in 1987, so many people crowded on that the deck changed shape. How?
slides.detail: Poor crowd control let roughly 300,000 people onto the bridge at once, and under their weight the centre span flattened out.

slides.question: Why did architect Irving Morrow choose the bridge’s orange colour?
options: It suits the setting and shows in fog
slides.explanation: Morrow picked the colour, known as International Orange, because it complements the natural surroundings, and it also makes the bridge easier to see in fog.
